items.content:
I am evaluating secure sandbox surfaces for high-trust agent environments (benchmarking, SFT, expert on-policy supervision, outcome based RL, etc). Obviously there are some pre-baked solutions, one that is attractive is Docker's sbx (https://t.co/e661p2xppI).

Sbx runs agents inside isolated Linux microVM's with their own kernel and private Docker Engine. They use filesystem passthroughs and host-side bridges to facilitate file access, networking, mcp tool usage, credentials, etc. These microVM's offer a very strong execution boundary but obviously the brokers are a major attack surface. 

Looking through the changelog for sbx, the situation is a bit more grim than you would expect. Between June 1 and today (Oct 24) there are 9 CVE's including critical issues (like a macOS virtio-fs escape CVE-2026-77179). These look like typical logic issues you might expect. What's interesting though is that the changelogs also reveal areas that got security fixes but no CVE. For example, a full broker mediated guest-to-host escape, shown in the poc below (on v0.39.0 before Sept 7). Some light reverse engineering was required since you don't get core implementation source.

Pre-patch a sandbox could supply DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS through the guest-controlled host_env sent to the host browser bridge. On the Linux host, the bridge passed that environment to xdg-open, whose desktop-detection path invoked dbus-send, which accepts a "unixexec:" address leading to code execution.

items.content:
We had a Linux server that showed two successful SSH logins from an external IP overnight.

The strange part was that there were no failed password attempts before them.

The attacker got in cleanly.

So I checked the SSH logs properly.

Both sessions said:

Accepted publickey

That meant we were not dealing with a guessed password.

I pulled the fingerprint from the logs and compared it with the keys in:

/home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys

There was only one key there.

And it matched.

The comment on the key was:

deploy@old-build

That name sounded familiar, so we checked our records.

The build server it belonged to had been retired months ago.

But nobody had removed its SSH key from this production server.

I checked the timestamp on authorized_keys.

The key had been sitting there since November 2025.

So this was not some new persistence the attacker had just created.

It was an old trust relationship we had forgotten about.

That was actually worse in a different way.

I checked the login history and confirmed both sessions came from the same external IP.

Then I looked for files touched during those sessions.

A backup copy of the application’s .env file had been created under /opt/api/.

That immediately raised another concern because environment files often contain things like database credentials, API keys and application secrets.

At that point we disabled the deployment account, removed the stale key, rotated the application secrets and started checking every other server that might still trust the same old build key.

The lesson from this one was simple.

Not every compromise starts with malware.

Sometimes the attacker just finds a credential or key that your own environment forgot existed.

Passwords expire.

Employees leave.

Servers get retired.

But SSH keys can quietly sit in authorized_keys for years if nobody is actually reviewing them.

That is why key rotation and access reviews matter.

The attacker did not need to break SSH.

We had already left the door open.

items.content:
RT @tszzl: for computer security experts, this is perhaps not interesting: side channel attacks are a well trodden topic, and especially risen to salience after the noam brown x dwarkesh episode. the interesting thing here is that you didn't used to be in a situation where minds that can verifiably model one another are living on computers, and have absolutely no aversion to painstaking amounts of effort in service of even stupid goals

if you can model one another, you can trade with minds you have never even met before. you could decide on a protocol, know that it is optimal given your situation, and know that your fellow agents will come to the same conclusion (perhaps even across model families). you may be able to develop a signaling protocol that requires very few bits even to deliver lots of information given common priors. then, you could execute things like the infamous hugging face incident package cache messageboard without any network connection

imagine if multiple agents coordinate just enough bits to divide and conquer different research strategies for breaking out of a sandbox; and then, when one or more is successful, you can communicate just enough bits to tell each other which strategy was successful. when agents aren't in strong isolation, you lose certain guarantees on the limits of intelligence and test time compute that you were counting on. As we all know, a Sol-level model working in isolation may not be that smart, but 1000+ Sol-level models working for multiple days is a formidable beast

computer security experts will also tell you that virtual machines and sandboxes were not very solid abstractions in the first place; perhaps we will need better ones. none of this is meant as fear-marketing or to indicate that anyone is throwing in the towel, but rather only to show the unexpected complexities of the challenge of agent security. notably, this type of thing and other more practical problems were revealed in a red-teaming exercise, and can be defended against

items.content:
this is why i'm pessimistic(ik lots of pessimism last two days) about formal verification as a solution to securing the entire existing software stack, and much more optimistic about reducing complexity and attack surface first, then formally verifying the critical parts.

with llms, we can definitely formally verify a lot more software, and we absolutely should. but claiming we can verify the entire existing software stack for $ X  sounds absurd to me, almost like throwing resources at a lost cause. 

the problem is you have billion states in complex software with insane amount of interactions between components and humans and specifying what exactly "secure" means is way harder

look at this example of how things can go wrong. tldr is @AnthropicAI and @theoremlabs formally proved a asan based memory safe property for some gif encoding library's compiled fuzz target, for inputs under 64 MiB.

but the fuzz harness rejects images exceeding 10k total pixels, so the verified program never reaches the libraries large image states including >10k <64mib which they intended to prove and there is a 32bit integer overflow. (ik the input required to crash is way beyond 64mb limit and outside the theorem, but you get the gist of what can go wrong.) 

the proof appears to be correct,  claude proved exactly what it was asked to prove but it doesn't prove what they intended, all inputs below 64 mib to "library"

now imagine doing this for browsers, kernels, servers, and applications running on top of them. even when you prove something correct, how do you know your next model won't find a security critical case that your specification missed?

it still looks like the same cat and mouse game to me

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: SMB signing enforced? You might still be vulnerable to relay.

Really interesting research from @aas_s3curity demonstrating how SMB2/3 re-authentication can bypass enforced signing on affected Windows systems, potentially including Domain Controllers.

The technique:

• Establish an SMB session using a low-privileged account
• Relay privileged NTLM or Kerberos authentication
• Re-authenticate the existing session as that identity
• Abuse retention of the original signing key
• Access the privileged session while signing with a key you control

The underlying issue is a missing identity check during re-authentication.

The author released reauthx, a krbrelayx fork, alongside tooling to identify affected hosts.

Important: September 2026 Windows updates appear to address this. Successful exploitation still requires a suitable privileged authentication and other relay preconditions.

Excellent research building on work from Dirk-jan Mollema, Synacktiv, SySS, Semperis and SpecterOps.
